gaps.sentence: She speaks ___ Spanish and Italian fluently.
gaps.explanation: 'Both ... and ...' links two items affirmatively; 'neither/either' pair with 'nor/or'.

gaps.sentence: This year the festival attracted ___ visitors than in 2024.
gaps.explanation: 'Fewer' is the comparative for countable plurals like visitors; 'less' is for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: ___ of my two brothers work in banking.
gaps.explanation: 'Both of my two brothers work ...' is correct; 'all' and 'none' are not used for two.

gaps.sentence: ___ words, the plan is too expensive.
gaps.explanation: 'In other words' is the fixed phrase for rephrasing; 'another' cannot modify the plural 'words'.

gaps.sentence: She carried a suitcase in ___ hand.
gaps.explanation: 'Each hand' views the two hands individually; 'every hand' is not used for body parts this way.

gaps.sentence: I haven't got ___ cash on me — I'll pay by card.
gaps.explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in negative sentences; 'haven't got no cash' would be a double negative.

gaps.sentence: She has ___ patience with excuses; deliver on time or do not bother coming.
gaps.explanation: 'Has no patience with' — 'no' directly negates the noun.
'Several charges' means more than two; the other options are used only with uncountable nouns.
